To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the IGT is a task in which the participant is presented with two options, each with a different long-term payoff.

(a), in the Iowa Gambling Test, the decision-making phase can be carried out while the participant performs an unrelated task; (b), the decision-making phase does not require learning; (c), the decision-making process can be dissociated from the learning process; (d), the decision-making and learning processes are both sensitive to losses; and (e), the decision-making is sensitive to losses in the same way as the learning process.

(i) two dissociable processes underlie decisions in the IGT, (ii) one of these is sensitive to the frequency of losses and the other to long-term payoffs, and (iii) the two processes interact with each in different ways.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the mechanisms underlying human decision making.
the study of the mechanisms of learning and decision making.
the cognitive processes that underlie decision making, and the factors that affect these processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the IGT is not a single task but rather a collection of several tasks that can be used to study different aspects of human decision making.
the IGT is a complex task, which is sensitive to many different aspects of cognition and emotion.

our results suggest that patients' deficits in the IGT may result from an impairment in allocating cognitive resources among different decision strategies, rather than a deficit in the ability to learn the long-term payoff of the options.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed a novel theoretical framework that can be used to explain performance in the Iowa gambling task and we have used it to explain the performance of patients with damage to the ventromedial cortex.
we have proposed and tested an integrative model for the IGT, and that this model can help us understand the impairments in this task in clinical populations.
the IGT is a complex task in which the decision process itself is not a unitary cognitive process but rather a combination of several dissociable processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, to understand the nature of decision making impairments, it is crucial to understand the cognitive processes that underlie normal performance.
the cognitive processes involved in the Iowa Gambling task are not unitary, and that different cognitive processes are likely to be impaired in different patient groups.
a better understanding of the cognitive processes involved in decision making can lead to a better understanding of patients' impairments and to more effective rehabilitation strategies.
